analysis.one_liner: Creates paid family leave insurance, paid sick days, expanded child care, universal prekindergarten, and free school breakfasts.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: with 60 House Democrats backing it, it sat in four committees for the rest of the Congress and died when that Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The Balancing Act was a package of pro-family workplace laws. It would create a social insurance program paying workers up to 12 weeks of partial-wage leave for a new baby, a serious illness, or a family member's care, funded by a small payroll premium split between workers and employers. It would require many employers to provide paid sick days, extend unpaid family leave to smaller employers, and add leave for school events, routine medical appointments, and domestic violence situations. It would also expand federal funding for child care, teacher scholarships and health coverage, universal prekindergarten, free school breakfast for all children regardless of income, and benefits for part-time and contract workers.
analysis.who_benefits: Working parents and caregivers, especially low-wage workers: an employee earning $20,000 or less would get 100% of pay during leave, sliding down to 40% for the highest earners. The paid sick leave and expanded leave provisions cover workers at firms with 25 or more employees; part-time, leased, and contract workers gain pension and health plan coverage. Child care providers gain scholarships, health coverage, and facilities grants; families with young children gain care subsidies, pre-K, and school breakfast.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal Family and Medical Insurance Program paying eligible employees up to 12 workweeks of benefits for births, adoptions, serious health conditions, and family care, with a benefit of 100% of daily earnings for workers making $20,000 or less, phased down to 40% for the highest earners [S2] [S3].

Funds the program through a family and medical leave premium of 0.2% of wages paid equally by employees and employers (0.1% for participating small employers), deposited in a dedicated Family and Medical Leave Insurance Fund in the Treasury [S3].

Requires covered employers to provide paid sick time, bars them from discriminating against workers who use it, and extends FMLA coverage to employers with 25 or more employees instead of 50 [S2] [S3].

Adds FMLA leave for school participation and routine family medical needs (up to 24 hours a year), leave for domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking, and includes same-sex spouses and domestic partners under FMLA [S2] [S3].

Expands child care funding for children under three, creates provider development grants and scholarships plus health coverage for child care workers, authorizes facilities financing grants, and provides business incentives for employer-run child care [S2] [S3].

Authorizes grants for universal full-day prekindergarten for all three-, four-, and five-year-olds, requires free school breakfasts regardless of family income, and removes income-restrictions on 21st century afterschool program applications [S2] [S3].

Treats part-time workers as full-time for pension participation, vesting, and accrual rules, qualifies them for group health plans, and extends ERISA to certain leased and contracted workers [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers pay a 0.2% payroll premium (0.1% for participating small employers) on top of the employee-side premium paid by workers through payroll deduction, and employers with 15 or more employees must provide paid sick time. Self-employed participants pay a 0.4% premium. Employers also face compliance and enforcement costs, including damages and attorney fees for interfering with leave rights.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers and workers via payroll premiums

drawbacks.text: The bill is financed by a new mandatory payroll premium of 0.2% on both employees and employers, a real cost on every covered wage; supporters argue it is modest, but it adds to labor costs at a time of high unemployment following the recession [S3].

The paid sick time mandate applies to employers with 15 or more employees and the leave mandates carry employer compliance burdens, and opponents argued such mandates make hiring more expensive; the bill allows employers with equivalent plans to opt out, which preserves private alternatives but complicates enforcement [S2] [S3].

The package bundles many separate programs (leave insurance, sick leave, child care grants, pre-K, school breakfast, pension rules) into one bill, so a member had to accept all of it or none, limiting room for compromise [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and targeted at people with the least flexibility: paid leave and sick days are standard in nearly every other industrialized nation, and the bill's findings note 78% of workers who need leave skip it because they cannot afford it. The costs are real but modest and explicitly priced: a 0.2% split payroll premium plus sick-day mandates for mid-size and larger employers. The design is fairly careful, with a progressive benefit formula, waiting period, fraud penalties, voluntary-plan alternatives, and small-employer accommodations.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees the day it was introduced, sent to two subcommittees, and no committee ever voted on it; it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Lynn Woolsey introduced the Balancing Act of 2011 on June 23, 2011, joined by 28 original cosponsors including Reps. George Miller, Rosa DeLauro, and Pete Stark [S1] [S3].
The bill was referred the same day to four committees: Education and the Workforce, Oversight and Government Reform, House Administration, and Ways and Means [S5].

On June 30, 2011 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Federal Workforce, U.S. Postal Service, and Labor Policy, and on September 8, 2011 to the Subcommittee on Early Childhood, Elementary, and Secondary Education; no further action was ever taken [S5].

The bill gathered 59 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, for a total of 60 House supporters, but it never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any Senate counterpart action, and expired at the end of the 112th Congress on January 3, 2013 [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have paid the new payroll premiums and provided paid sick days are better off, since the requirements never took effect. Workers who needed paid leave, sick days, child care, or pre-K gained nothing.

for.name: Lynn Woolsey
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-CA), bill sponsor, retired at the end of the Congress
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 28 original cosponsors across its leave, child care, education, and workplace provisions

for.name: 59 of 193 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it 60 total House supporters, all Democrats

against.name: John Kline
against.role: Chair, House Education and Workforce Committee (112th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Led the primary committee of referral and never brought the bill to a markup or vote before the Congress ended

against.name: John Boehner
against.what_they_did: Controlled the House floor schedule and never allowed the bill to come to a vote, and referred it to four committees where it stalled

sides.party_line_note: All 59 cosponsors were Democrats in a House controlled by a 242-seat Republican majority, and no committee or floor action followed; no Republicans supported the bill on the record.

industries.industry: Covered employers (businesses with 15 or more employees)
industries.note: Employers would pay a 0.2% payroll premium and must provide paid sick time and comply with leave protections, with damages and attorney fees for violations. The employer premium also functions as the funding source for workers' benefits, so the industry's cost is the public's gain.

Employers opting for a voluntary equivalent plan must purchase insurance from an admitted disability insurer approved by the Secretary of Labor, creating a new market for private leave insurance alongside the public program.

Providers gain federal funding for expansion, health benefits coverage, development grants, scholarships, and facilities financing, which raises care quality and wages in a sector where teachers averaged about $20,940 a year.
Certified CDFIs and similar organizations would receive competitive grants for acquiring, building, or renovating child care facilities.
